items.title: 52300_Trummy Young oral history interview
items.q: And when I play with guys like Waters, and Watrous Rosalino, you know, and them, well,

ctx.x: Yeah, you would. I find it to be true. But naturally, if you -- most guys, if they're going to do something real important you like to have a guy that know what you're doing. But when you're with pros -- when you're with the real pros, they can do what you're doing. They might have a little different twist to the way they do it, you know.

I find it real challenging -- I find it real challenging to really play with guys that you haven't been playing with all the time. And when I play with guys like Waters, and Watrous Rosalino, you know, and them, well,

they play altogether different from what I play. You know, my style is more the swing style and they're real up on top of the modern thing. And I enjoy what they're doing. And, of course, it doesn't make me change my way of playing. It's just the contrast in the playing, you know. But I enjoy doing things like that. And --

items.title: Bill Watrous interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 26, 1999

ctx.x: Oh yeah. We didn’t really talk about maybe just a few of your influences, on the trombone, besides your father. You mentioned a couple of influences, Lou McGarrity or did you sub for him?

I subbed for Cutty Cutshall, that’s who I subbed for, but I knew Lou and Lou was a wonderful trombone player. Vic Dickinson was one of my favs at that time, and Trummy Young I loved. Of course Urbie Green and J.J., to say nothing of Frankie Rosolino and Carl, Carl Fontana frankly for me is my all together hands down favorite of them all. I don’t think there’s anyone today on the scene that is a match for Carl Fontana. He is incredible. Absolutely. Great trombone player.
Okay, so I don’t usually ask this question, but if you tried to be real honest about where you fit in the list of trombone players—
